sources.entry: jlevy/the-art-of-command-line: master the command line, in one page must read

summary.one_liner: A one-page, link-free guide of practical command-line tips and tools, mostly for Bash on Linux, aimed at both beginners and experienced users.
summary.what_it_does: The guide is a long bulleted list organized into sections: Basics, Everyday use, Processing files and data, System debugging, One-liners, Obscure but useful, macOS only, Windows only, and More resources. It covers interactive Bash keybindings, job control, redirection, globbing and quoting, ssh key-based login, and file and disk management commands such as ls, find, du, and ln. It also covers text and data tools like grep, sort/uniq, awk, sed, jq, rsync, and xargs, plus Bash scripting safety settings (set -euo pipefail, trap). Diagnostics are covered too: strace, lsof, ss, iostat, vmstat, mtr, and /proc. Platform-specific notes for macOS (brew, pbcopy, BSD differences) and Windows (Cygwin, WSL, MinGW) are included. Most entries are one-line pointers to a tool, with short examples where useful.
use_cases: finding and processing text or data files from the terminal
debugging a slow or misbehaving Linux system
syncing or copying files with rsync
looking up which process is listening on a port
notable: Covers both everyday interactive shell use and scripting safety tips in one page
Includes a categorized list of obscure but useful Unix commands with one-line descriptions
Has separate macOS-only and Windows-only sections explaining Cygwin, WSL and BSD differences
Translated into many languages, with the README listing over a dozen language versions
caveats: Written mainly for Linux and Bash; some commands differ on macOS (BSD) and Windows
Mostly names tools and commands without full explanations, and says it relies on readers looking up details elsewhere
The author states it is seeking a new co-author to expand it into a more comprehensive guide
